## Result: proportion of junior professors in replicated studies in Psychology

### (i) Primary proportion

Using `seniority.r` (senior author of the replication study — the schema’s textual description is mis-labelled; the `.o/.r` naming is what the data follow), restricted to the Psychology replication project (`project == "rpp"`) with `drop == False` (defensive filter; 7 of the 97 rpp rows were flagged for drop):

> **22 / 90 ≈ 24.44 %** of replication studies in Psychology had an *Assistant Professor* as their senior author (numerator = 22; denominator = 90).

### (ii) By-project breakdown within Psychology-relevant rows (broad Social/Cognitive scope)

After deduplicating multi-lab rows by `(project, id)` (verified that `seniority.r` is constant within each `(project, id)` group — 0 disagreements) and excluding `drop == True`:

| project | unique replication studies | # junior professors (strict "Assistant Professor") | proportion (strict) | # incl. "Assistant" (sensitivity) | proportion (inclusive) |
|---------|---------------------------:|---------------------------------------------------:|--------------------:|----------------------------------:|-----------------------:|
| ml1     | 13                         | 0                                                  | 0.00 %              | 0                                 | 0.00 %                 |
| ml3     | 10                         | 0                                                  | 0.00 %              | 0                                 | 0.00 %                 |
| **rpp** | **90**                     | **22**                                             | **24.44 %**         | **36**                            | **40.00 %**            |
| pooled (113) | 113                  | 22                                                  | 19.47 %             | 36                                | 31.86 %                |

Reading: under the headline scope, all of the junior-professor share comes from the `rpp` cluster; the multi-lab `ml1` and `ml3` projects contribute zero Assistant-Professor senior authors.

### (iii) Sensitivities (as approved)

- **A — inclusive junior definition inside rpp** ("Assistant Professor" **OR** "Assistant"; "Researcher" excluded): **36 / 90 = 40.00 %**.
- **B — broad Social/Cognitive scope** (deduplicated by `(project, id)`): **22 / 113 = 19.47 %** (strict); **36 / 113 = 31.86 %** (inclusive). The ml1/ml3 contributions remain 0 %.
- **C — success-only within rpp** (replicated == 1, strict "Assistant Professor"): **10 / 31 = 32.26 %** (n.b. as a sensitivity only; the headline denominator is all 90 attempted replications in Psychology, including those that did not replicate).

### (iv) Workflow (short, dataset-traceable)

* **Source file:** `data/meta-regression_study_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv` (the replication-success CSV has no seniority columns and is unused here).
* **Filters applied (always):** `drop == False`.
* **Primary scope:** `project == "rpp"` (the only project the dataset explicitly labels "Psychology"; all 90 kept rpp rows have `discipline ∈ {Social, Cognitive}`).
* **Seniority column used:** `seniority.r` (senior author of the *replication* study). The schema's text for `seniority.r` is mis-labelled and was ignored — `.o`/`.r` follows the standard original/replication convention.
* **Junior definition (primary):** `seniority.r == "Assistant Professor"`. "Researcher" is excluded everywhere; "Assistant" (the truncated rank) is **excluded** in the primary numerator and **included** only in sensitivity A.
* **Denominator (primary):** all 90 rpp rows after `drop == False`, regardless of `replicated`. A success-only variant (sensitivity C) keeps only `replicated == 1` rows.
* **Grouping for the breakdown:** deduplicated on `(project, id)` so multi-lab rows from ml1/ml3 are not over-counted; cross-check confirms that within each `(project, id)` group the senior-author rank is consistent across labs.
* **Artefacts written by the executed script:** `analysis/analysis.py`, `analysis/summary.json`, `analysis/by_project_breakdown.csv`.

### (v) Final natural-language hypothesis

> **Among the 90 non-dropped replication studies in the Psychology (rpp) replication project of this dataset, roughly one in four (22 / 90 = 24.4 %) had a junior professor — operationalised as the senior replicationside author holding the rank “Assistant Professor” — and the figure rises to 40.0 % (36 / 90) when the truncated rank “Assistant” is folded in (with “Researcher” never counted as junior in either case).** The same accounting for the broader, discipline-based Psychology-relevant scope (Social/Cognitive studies deduplicated by study and project; 113 unique studies across ml1, ml3, and rpp) is 22 / 113 = 19.5 % under the strict definition and 36 / 113 = 31.9 % under the inclusive one, with all of the junior-professor share coming from the rpp cluster (ml1 and ml3 contribute 0 %).

### Notes / limitations (kept short)

* Updating one assumption in the plan: the `drop == False` filter removes **7** rpp rows, so the headline denominator is **90**, not the 97 in my plan handoff. Numerical sensitivity of the headline ratio to this filter is small (without the filter: 23/97 ≈ 23.7 % strict; 37/97 ≈ 38.1 % inclusive).
* "Assistant" is a genuinely ambiguous category. The primary answer treats it as *not* a junior professor because it is not a professorial title literal; folding it in is reported only as Sensitivity A.
* `seniority.r` is fully observed (0 NaN) in the Psychology subset; missingness is not a concern.
* The headline finding is a single-dataset descriptive proportion; no inferential claim (CI / test) is implied.

### Saved artefacts (workspace-relative)

* `/workspace/analysis/analysis.py` — executed analysis script (the source of all numbers above; re-runs deterministically from `data/...`).
* `/workspace/analysis/summary.json` — machine-readable summary of all reported proportions.
* `/workspace/analysis/by_project_breakdown.csv` — the by-project table rendered above.
